subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage: Omkar was waiting for the canteen queue when he noticed Tushar at the next table, holding a printout of his project report while the group leader spoke. Tushar's shoulders had gone up for a second, then dropped. He took out a pen and asked, "Which section felt weakest, the method or the results?" The leader said the results were rushed and the charts were unlabelled. Tushar wrote both down. Then the leader said, "And honestly your whole approach is lazy." Tushar paused. "The charts I can fix by Friday. I don't think lazy is right, since I redid the survey twice. But I'll show you the new version." Omkar couldn't tell if the comment still stung, but Tushar stayed seated and kept writing.

qa.q: Which two problems did the leader name in the results section?
qa.a: The leader said the results were rushed and the charts were unlabelled.

qa.q: What does Tushar's pause and his question about the weakest section suggest about how he took the criticism, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggests he was steadying himself and wanted to learn, though the dropped shoulders show it may still have stung.

qa.q: What could Tushar try if he wanted the leader to see his effort?
qa.a: He could bring the revised charts and the two versions of the survey by Friday so the leader can see the work directly.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Tushar's response compared with snapping back or agreeing to everything?
qa.a: Omkar probably sees it as steadier, since Tushar took the useful points and calmly disagreed with the unfair one.

grounding: An observer sees Tushar ask clarifying questions and separate useful from unfair criticism.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage:
Day one. Tushar got his first internship review back from Ganga, his supervisor, and read it standing at the printer. Her notes said his reports were late and the summaries too long. He typed a reply full of reasons, then deleted it. He wrote instead: "Thank you. Could you show me one summary you think is the right length?"

Three days later they sat together. Ganga pointed to a two-line summary and explained what she kept and cut. Tushar said the lateness was fair, but the long summaries were partly because he hadn't known who read them. Ganga admitted she should have told him.

Two weeks later Tushar's summary went out in half the length. He walked to the bus with his back a little straighter, thinking he could use a note like that again. 🙂

qa.q: What did Tushar ask Ganga to show him?
qa.a: He asked her to show him one summary she thought was the right length.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he deleted his first reply, and why?
qa.a: He likely felt defensive at first, and deleting the reasons suggests he wanted to listen rather than protect himself.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking for an example worked, because it gave him something concrete to copy and led to a talk where both sides shared what they had missed.

qa.q: What might Ganga have been thinking when Tushar mentioned he hadn't known who read the summaries?
qa.a: Ganga probably realised her own instructions were unclear, and she admitted it, which shows the feedback could go both ways.

grounding: Tushar receives criticism, asks clarifying questions, accepts the fair points and explains the unfair one over several days.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage: Nandini, you came to me upset about your manager's comments, so let your Kashish didi tell you about my first performance review, at twenty-three. My manager, Mr Rao, said my reports were "sloppy" and I "didn't take initiative". My face went hot. I wanted to argue: I'd stayed late every Friday for months! Instead I sat there saying, "Yes, sir, sorry, sir," and went home and cried, sure I was useless. I didn't sleep. Next day, my senior Lata said, "Did you ask him what he meant?" I hadn't. So I went back with a notebook. "Sir, which reports were sloppy?" He showed me two with wrong totals. Fair. "And initiative, can you give an example?" He couldn't really; he'd confused me with someone else. So I took the first point, fixed my checks, and told him politely the second didn't fit. He actually agreed.

qa.q: What did Mr Rao show young Kashish when asked which reports were sloppy?
qa.a: Two reports with wrong totals.

qa.q: How did young Kashish feel after the first review?
qa.a: She felt hurt and hopeless, crying at home and sure she was useless, instead of seeing what was fair and what wasn't.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Kashish learn from the review?
qa.a: Going back with a notebook and asking Mr Rao for examples, which separated the fair point about totals from the unfair one about initiative.

qa.q: How did Mr Rao respond when Kashish questioned the initiative comment?
qa.a: He couldn't give a real example and agreed, since he had confused her with someone else.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from total self-blame to asking clarifying questions and separating fair criticism from unfair.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage: The college drama script was due at the festival office by six, and it was already 4:45. Hemant, the director, flipped through Dhruv's pages in the noisy rehearsal hall. "The second scene drags. And honestly, the ending is cheesy." Dhruv felt the heat rise in his face. He'd spent three nights on that ending. His mouth opened to snap back. He shut it. With an hour left, a fight would waste the time. "Okay. Which part of scene two drags? Can you point to lines?" Hemant tapped a long speech. "Here. The mother repeats herself." Dhruv read it. Fair. He cut six lines. "And the ending, is it the words or the idea?" Hemant thought. "The idea's fine. The last line just spells it out." Dhruv crossed out the final line. It was stronger. They submitted at 5:52. The cheesy remark still stung, but the script was better.

qa.q: What time did they submit the script?
What was Dhruv feeling when Hemant called the ending cheesy?
qa.a: He felt stung and angry, the heat rising in his face after three nights of work; he wanted to snap back.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that turned the criticism into something useful?
qa.a: He held back his reaction and asked clarifying questions about exact lines and whether the problem was the words or the idea.

qa.q: How might Hemant have seen Dhruv's questions?
qa.a: He probably saw them as a sign that Dhruv could take feedback, which made it easier to give a precise and fair answer.

grounding: Shows a young adult taking criticism under time pressure without bristling, asking clarifying questions and keeping what is useful.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage: At the quarterly review in the Bengaluru office, Nazia went through Pranav's work. "Your client emails are excellent. Clear and polite. But your code reviews are slow, sometimes three days, and the team waits. And I've heard you're not a team player." Pranav's chest tightened. The last one felt unfair; he'd covered two colleagues' shifts last month. For a second he wanted to shrink into his chair and say sorry for everything. He breathed. "Thank you about the emails. On the code reviews, you're right. Can we agree on a target, maybe one day?" Nazia nodded. "On the team-player point, can you tell me where that came from? Last month I covered for Arjun and Sneha twice." Nazia paused and checked her notes. "Fair. That came from one person, and I hadn't looked into it. I'll take it out." Pranav left with one clear goal and his shoulders loose.

qa.q: How long do Pranav's code reviews sometimes take?
qa.a: Sometimes three days.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when Nazia said he wasn't a team player?
qa.a: He felt tense and hurt, his chest tightening, because the comment seemed unfair given he had covered colleagues' shifts.

qa.q: How did Pranav separate the fair criticism from the unfair one?
qa.a: He accepted the code review point and suggested a target, and calmly asked where the team-player comment came from, offering evidence.

qa.q: How did Nazia respond when Pranav questioned the team-player comment?
qa.a: She checked her notes, admitted it came from one person she hadn't looked into, and agreed to take it out.

grounding: Shows a young adult taking feedback without shrinking or bristling, asking questions and separating useful points from unfair ones.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage:
In the small meeting room at the research centre, Nilesh tapped the printout.
"I've read your internship report. Honestly? The analysis is weak, and the whole thing reads like you rushed it."
Gurpreet breathed out slowly. "Okay. Can you show me where the analysis falls short?"
"Page six. You list the survey numbers but never say what they mean for the shop owners."
"That's fair. I can add a paragraph on that. What made it feel rushed?"
"The typos, mainly. And the formatting."
"The typos, yes, I'll fix them. But the fieldwork took three weeks. Is it the writing that feels rushed, or the research?"
Nilesh paused. "The writing. The fieldwork's actually solid."
"Thanks, that helps. So: what the numbers on page six mean, and a proper proofread. Anything else?"
"No. Send it on Friday."
That evening Gurpreet's sister phoned to ask how it went. "My first instinct was to argue, or to feel useless," Gurpreet said. "I did neither. I asked questions."

qa.q: On which page did Nilesh find the analysis weak?
qa.a: Page six.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet tempted to feel when the criticism came?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt the pull to argue defensively or to feel useless, but steadied with a slow breath.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet separate the useful points from the unfair one?
qa.a: By asking clarifying questions: accepting the page-six point and the typos, and asking whether "rushed" meant the writing or the research, which showed the fieldwork was solid.

qa.q: How did Nilesh's view shift during the talk?
qa.a: Nilesh moved from calling the whole report rushed to admitting the fieldwork was solid and only the writing needed work.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult taking criticism by listening, asking clarifying questions and separating useful points from unfair ones, without bristling or self-blame.
